Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the UniBank Group third quarter Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, instructions for queuing up will be given at that time. Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera:
Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to review UniBank Group's results for the third quarter. With me this morning are Sarah Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; Michael Chen, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Patel, Chief Risk Officer; and David Kim, Chief Credit Officer.

Before we begin, let me remind you that some of the statements we will be making today are forward-looking. These statements are based on current expectations and assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a discussion of these factors.

I will now turn the call over to Sarah Thompson.

Sarah Thompson:
Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. UniBank Group delivered strong performance in the third quarter, driven by our commitment to customer service and operational excellence.

Our key priorities for this year remain focused on:
1. Growing our core businesses
2. Investing in technology and innovation
3. Managing risk effectively
4. Optimizing our capital allocation
5. Enhancing our employee engagement.

Now, I'd like to provide some highlights on a few key areas. Our capital ratios strengthened meaningfully, with CET1 at 14.2%, well above targets and regulatory requirements. Revenue diversification initiatives continued to gain traction, shifting our mix toward more stable fee income. Despite choppy market conditions, non-interest income showed resilience on an adjusted basis. We're making excellent progress on our key strategic initiatives, particularly in digital transformation and market expansion. And our capital return plans remain shareholder-friendly, with robust dividends and buybacks.

I will now turn the call over to Michael Chen to discuss our financial results in more detail.

Michael Chen:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning. UniBank Group reported net income of $2.1 billion for the third quarter, or $1.42 per share. Our results reflect strong revenue growth, disciplined expense management, and a healthy credit environment.

Net interest income increased 11% year-over-year due to loan growth and improved net interest margin, which expanded 12 basis points quarter-over-quarter to 3.45%. Non-interest income was $2.8 billion, up 18% year-over-year on an adjusted basis and reflecting record contributions from key franchises. Key performance indicators include an ROE of 15.4% and an efficiency ratio of 54.2%. We are confident in our ability to achieve our financial goals for the year.

Before diving into segment performance, let me provide a comprehensive update on our capital ratios, which remain a cornerstone of our fortress balance sheet and a key differentiator in this highly regulated industry. Maintaining robust CET1 and Tier 1 ratios not only ensures compliance with evolving global standards but also positions us to pursue value-accretive growth opportunities, including organic expansion, selective M&A, and returning capital to shareholders via dividends and buybacks.

At the end of Q3, our Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio stood at 14.2% on a fully loaded Basel III basis, up 40 basis points quarter-over-quarter and 120 basis points year-over-year. This places us well above our internal target range of 12.5-13.5% and significantly ahead of regulatory minima. Our Tier 1 ratio was 15.8%, reflecting a similar trajectory with a 30 basis points quarter-over-quarter increase. For context, these levels compare favorably to peers: JPMorgan's CET1 at around 15.0%, HSBC's at 14.5%, and Wells Fargo's at 11.8% post their recent CCAR approval.

We're operating in a multi-jurisdictional landscape shaped by Basel III endgame reforms, which are being phased in globally. Under Pillar 1, the minimum CET1 requirement is 4.5%, but with the capital conservation buffer at 2.5%, that's effectively 7.0%. For UniBank, as a G-SIB—Global Systemically Important Bank—we face an additional 1.5% G-SIB surcharge, bringing the headline requirement to 8.5%. Add our countercyclical buffer (CCyB) at 0.5% in the EU and 0% in the US, plus our Pillar 2A requirement of 2.8% from the ECB's SREP review earlier this year, and our all-in CET1 floor is approximately 11.8%. Tier 1 follows suit at around 13.3% fully loaded.

We're not just meeting these—we're exceeding them handily. Our CET1 fully loaded excess over the all-in requirement is 2.4 percentage points, or roughly $18 billion in surplus capital, providing ample dry powder. On a transitional basis, which some peers still reference, our CET1 would be 15.1%, but we've proactively adopted full Basel III standards ahead of the January 2025 EU deadline and the US Basel III endgame proposal, expected to finalize with a 4.5% standardized CET1 floor plus buffers.

Key drivers of this quarter's strength include several organic and tactical factors. First, retained earnings contributed 60 basis points to CET1 accretion, fueled by our record $2.1 billion net income—EPS of $1.42, up 8% year-over-year—despite higher provisions for credit losses in our commercial real estate book amid office sector headwinds. Second, risk-weighted assets (RWAs) grew modestly by 1.2% quarter-over-quarter to $1.05 trillion, but our advanced IRB models for retail and corporate portfolios optimized RWA density, shaving 20 basis points off the denominator. We also executed $3.2 billion in share repurchases under our ongoing $10 billion program, authorized by the Fed post-CCAR, which reduced common shares outstanding by 1.1%.

Regionally, our US operations—40% of RWAs—saw CET1 phase-in at 14.8%, bolstered by strong consumer banking performance in mortgages and cards, where delinquencies remain below 1.0%. We've navigated the Fed's proposed Basel III endgame, which could add 10-20 basis points to RWAs via the expanded standardized approach for operational risk; our internal modeling suggests a negligible 5 basis points CET1 impact thanks to our diversified low-RWA fee businesses like wealth management. In Europe, comprising 35% of RWAs, our CET1 fully loaded ratio is 13.9%, comfortably above ECB requirements including the 1.0% Pillar 2B buffer. Recent EBA stress tests validated our resilience, with a fully loaded CET1 of 10.7% under the adverse scenario versus a 5.5% pass mark. Asia-Pacific, at 20% of RWAs, benefits from lighter APRA requirements in Australia (10.5% CET1 target) and HKMA's countercyclical stance, where our ratio hits 15.4%—ideal for supporting trade finance growth amid China recovery.

Strategically, we're laser-focused on capital optimization initiatives. We've launched a multi-year RWA efficiency program targeting 5-7% reduction by 2026 through portfolio deleveraging—e.g., selling $5 billion in non-core CRE loans—and advanced analytics for output floor mitigation under Basel IV. We're also exploring AT1 issuance; our $4 billion outstanding perpetuals yield competitively at SOFR + 425 basis points, and we could tap markets for $2-3 billion opportunistically to diversify Tier 1. On the regulatory front, we're actively engaging with the Fed on G-SIB scoring—our Short-Term Wholesale Funding score improved post-2023 reforms—potentially shaving 0.25% off our surcharge.

Looking forward, we expect CET1 to range 14.0-14.5% by year-end, assuming stable RWAs and mid-teens ROE. This positions us for a 10-15% dividend hike in Q1 2025, subject to approval, and further buybacks. In a higher-for-longer rate environment, our capital stack supports resilience against potential downturns, much like it did in 2020 when we ended with CET1 over 13% amid COVID stress.

This profile underscores UniBank's prudent risk management and shareholder alignment.

Good afternoon, everyone. Today, I'd like to dive deep into our revenue diversification initiatives and their tangible impact on our P&L—a strategic pillar that's delivering resilient growth amid the macroeconomic headwinds of persistent inflation, Fed rate uncertainty, and intensifying fintech disruption. In an era where net interest margins are volatile—our NIM expanded 12 basis points quarter-over-quarter to 3.45% but remains sensitive to deposit betas and loan repricing—diversifying away from traditional NII dependency is non-negotiable for sustainable ROE.

Three years ago, NII accounted for 68% of our total revenue. Fast-forward to Q3 2024, and we've shifted that mix to 52% NII and 48% non-interest income—a 16 percentage point pivot driven by disciplined execution across our three engines: Consumer & Business Banking (CBB), Wealth & Asset Management (WAM), and Corporate & Investment Banking (CIB). Non-interest revenue hit a record $2.8 billion in the quarter, up 18% year-over-year and 5% quarter-over-quarter, outpacing NII growth of 11% year-over-year. This diversification buffered our overall revenue growth at 14% year-over-year to $12.4 billion, even as we lapped tough comps from last year's rate surge.

Let's unpack the key initiatives and their impacts, segment by segment.

First, Wealth & Asset Management: our crown jewel for fee-based stability. WAM revenue surged 22% year-over-year to $1.1 billion, representing 39% of total non-interest income. Assets under management reached $620 billion, up 24% year-over-year, fueled by net new money inflows of $18 billion in Q3 alone—our best quarterly inflow since 2021. Strategically, we've accelerated our platform-agnostic model, akin to BlackRock's Aladdin ecosystem, by launching 'UniWealth AI,' our proprietary robo-advisory tool integrated with generative AI for hyper-personalized portfolio construction. This has driven 35% year-over-year growth in digital advisory assets to $45 billion, with client acquisition costs down 15% due to seamless CRM integrations via Salesforce and Plaid APIs.

Regionally, North America remains our bedrock at 55% of WAM revenue, but we're seeing explosive growth in Asia-Pacific, where AUM doubled to $120 billion. Our JV with a leading Singaporean sovereign wealth fund mirrors Temasek's playbook, capturing HNW inflows amid China's property stabilization. In Europe, MiFID II-compliant sustainable ETFs—now 18% of our ETF AUM—grew 28% year-over-year, positioning us ahead of peers like UBS in the ESG tailwind.

Second, Payments and Transaction Services: high-margin, volume-scaled growth. This franchise delivered $850 million in Q3 revenue, up 25% year-over-year, now 30% of non-interest income. Transaction volumes hit 4.2 billion, a 22% increase, propelled by our 'UniPay Nexus' platform—a real-time cross-border payments rail leveraging ISO 20022 standards and RippleNet-inspired blockchain settlement. We've reduced average settlement times from T+2 to near-instant for 70% of APAC-Europe flows, capturing 12% market share in emerging markets remittances.

Key technical initiative: embedding Visa Direct and our own tokenization layer for B2B payments, which boosted commercial card spend 30% year-over-year to $150 billion annualized. Margins here are elite at 65% versus CIB's 35%, and we're hedging FX volatility with proprietary algo trading desks. Regionally, U.S. consumer spending resilience—despite 4.1% unemployment—drove 15% volume growth, while India's UPI interoperability via our NPCI partnership added 40% year-over-year EM volume, outpacing competitors like HSBC in the subcontinent.

Third, Corporate & Investment Banking: cyclical counterbalance with advisory upside. CIB fees rose 14% year-over-year to $650 million, with investment banking fees up 19% on the back of a rebounding M&A pipeline—our advisory backlog now at $45 billion, echoing Goldman Sachs' momentum. Equity capital markets underwriting fees jumped 32% on three blockbuster IPOs, including a $2.5 billion tech listing, while debt capital markets benefited from high-yield issuance amid 5.25-5.50% Fed funds.

We've diversified within CIB by ramping sustainable finance—green bonds and transition loans now 22% of origination, up from 12% last year—aligning with ECB and PBOC mandates. FICC trading revenue was flat quarter-over-quarter at $300 million but up 8% year-over-year, supported by our quant-driven flow trading desk using ML models for volatility capture.

These initiatives aren't siloed; synergies amplify impact. For instance, CBB's 28 million digital customers—up 12% year-over-year—feed WAM and payments via embedded finance APIs, mirroring JPMorgan's Chase ecosystem. We've invested $450 million in 2024 CapEx for cloud-native core banking partnering with Temenos, enabling 40% faster product launches and reducing tech debt by 25%.

Risk-wise, we're stress-testing diversification under Basel IV scenarios, with non-interest income now covering 110% of operating expenses—up from 85% in 2022. Looking ahead, we guide 15-18% non-interest growth for FY24, targeting a 50/50 NII/non-interest mix by 2026. This positions UniBank with a superior fee-to-total revenue ratio of 48%, versus the KBW large-cap bank peer average of 42%, enhancing our CET1 buffer to 12.8%.

In summary, our diversification isn't just defensive—it's offensive, driving 250 basis points of ROE accretion YTD to 13.2%. We're built for whatever the yield curve throws at us.

I'll now turn to our non-interest income, which totaled $2.8 billion in the quarter, down 8% year-over-year but flat sequentially. Excluding a one-time $150 million gain from the sale of our legacy mortgage servicing portfolio last year, adjusted non-interest income grew 3% year-over-year, reflecting resilience amid a challenging macroeconomic backdrop. Let me unpack the key drivers, market impacts, and our strategic positioning across our key franchises: Consumer Banking, Corporate & Investment Banking (CIB), and Wealth & Asset Management (WAM).

Non-interest income represented 28% of our total revenue this quarter, down slightly from 32% a year ago due to the NIM expansion we've seen from higher-for-longer rates. But volatility in equity markets, a protracted slowdown in global M&A, and softening consumer sentiment have pressured fee-based revenues, partially offset by strength in trading and payments. Elevated interest rates—now at the Fed's 5.25-5.50% terminal range—have dampened capital markets activity, with global IPO volumes down 45% year-over-year per DealLogic data, mirroring trends at peers like JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs. Meanwhile, FX and rates volatility, driven by sticky inflation and Middle East geopolitical tensions, boosted our markets business.

Consumer non-interest income came in at $1.1 billion, up 2% year-over-year, led by record credit card fees of $650 million. Interchange revenue grew 12% on 7% card spend growth, fueled by our co-branded partnerships with Visa and Mastercard, and the rollout of our new UniBank Rewards Visa Infinite card, which saw 1.2 million new accounts in Q3. However, market conditions are showing cracks: deposit service charges dipped 5% to $250 million as fee waivers in our high-yield savings products—yielding 4.75% APY to compete with fintechs like Ally and SoFi—eroded overdraft income. Consumer confidence indices, per Conference Board data, fell to 98.7 in September, signaling potential pullback in discretionary spend.

Regionally, U.S. consumer fees remain robust at +5% year-over-year, supported by robust job markets in tech hubs like Austin and Raleigh-Durham. But in Europe, where we have $150 billion in deposits, fees declined 10% amid ECB rate cuts to 3.75% and regulatory caps on NSF fees under PSD3 directives. In Asia-Pacific, remittances and cross-border payments via our Zelle-like app grew 15%, but China's property sector woes curbed wealth transfer volumes.

Strategically, we're leaning into embedded finance: our API integrations with 500+ merchant platforms, including Shopify and Uber, generated $80 million in new transaction fees, up 40% quarter-over-quarter. We're also piloting AI-driven personalization with our "SmartFees" engine, which dynamically prices late fees to boost collections by 15% in beta tests.

CIB non-interest income fell sharply to $850 million, down 22% year-over-year, as market froth evaporated. Advisory fees plummeted 35% to $320 million, with completed M&A volumes at just $180 billion globally—half of 2021 peaks—per Refinitiv. Deal drought stems from antitrust scrutiny (e.g., FTC blocks on tech deals akin to Microsoft-Activision) and high financing costs; leveraged loan spreads widened to SOFR + 450 basis points, deterring LBOs. Underwriting fees dropped 18% to $210 million, hit by a 60% year-over-year plunge in U.S. high-yield issuance to $35 billion, as issuers await Fed cuts.

Bright spots: syndicated loans fees held steady at $150 million, bolstered by our #3 market share in investment-grade paper. Regionally, North America advisory was flat, but EMEA suffered a 40% drop from Basel IV implementation delays crimping Eurozone bank M&A. In APAC, our stronghold in Greater China outbound deals added $50 million, though Taiwan-China tensions capped momentum.

On trading desks, we posted a strong $170 million, up 25% year-over-year, from macro tailwinds. Rates trading revenue surged 40% on 10-year Treasury yield swings from 4.0% to 4.7%, while FX gained 15% on USD strength versus EUR (1.08) and JPY (145). Equities trading was mixed—prime brokerage up 10% on hedge fund flows, but cash equities flat amid Nasdaq volatility (VIX averaged 18). We've enhanced our electronic trading with Citadel Securities-inspired algorithms, capturing 25% of ADV in U.S. Treasuries via our QuantumFX platform, reducing latency to 50 microseconds.

WAM delivered $850 million, down 5% year-over-year but with $25 billion in net new money—our best Q3 since 2021. Recurring fees of $650 million (75 basis points on $350 billion AUM) benefited from higher equity betas, with S&P 500 up 18% YTD despite Q3's 5% pullback. Brokerage commissions rose 8% to $120 million on elevated retail trading volumes, echoing Robinhood-era activity but with our institutional-grade tools.

Market headwinds: private market fundraising slowed 20% per Preqin, hitting our $50 billion alternatives franchise. Ultra-high-net-worth outflows in Europe ($2 billion) tied to deglobalization fears post-Ukraine war. Positively, U.S. advisor productivity hit record $2.5 million per RIA, up 10%, via our WealthConnect CRM upgrade with Salesforce Einstein AI for lead scoring.

Looking ahead, we expect non-interest income of $2.7-2.9 billion in Q4, implying modest growth if M&A rebounds with anticipated 25-50 basis points Fed cuts. Key risks: prolonged high rates could sustain capex caution, pressuring IB fees 10-15% into 2025, per Goldman Sachs forecasts. Upside from volatility: our macro franchise is positioned for VIX spikes above 20.

Strategically, we're diversifying beyond cycles: first, fintech acceleration—$500 million invested in partnerships like Plaid for open banking and Stripe for B2B payments, targeting $300 million incremental revenue by 2026. Second, data & AI monetization—launching "UniBank Insights" analytics-as-a-service for corporates, leveraging our 10 petabytes of transaction data for predictive FX hedging, akin to Bloomberg Terminal 2.0. Third, regional tailoring—doubling down on U.S. cards (aiming 10% share in premium segment) and APAC custody ($200 billion target AuC). Fourth, risk-adjusted growth—maintaining 95% client satisfaction via ESG-integrated products, capturing $10 trillion in sustainable flows per Morningstar.

While market torpidity challenged non-interest income, our diversified model and tech investments buffered the downside. We're executing on a path to 5-7% CAGR through the cycle, outpacing peers.

Before I move on, let me provide an update on our key strategic initiatives and the tangible progress we're making. Our strategy is anchored in four pillars: accelerating digital transformation, enhancing customer-centric growth, expanding in high-potential markets, and embedding sustainable resilience. These initiatives are delivering measurable results amid a dynamic macro environment—persistent inflation at 3.2% globally, Fed funds rate steady at 5.25-5.50%, and deposit betas stabilizing at around 2.8% for our peers.

Digital transformation, our highest priority, now accounts for 28% of our overall R&D spend, up from 22% last year. We've made significant strides in our cloud-native core banking platform migration, partnering with AWS and FIS to complete 65% of our retail and commercial banking portfolios by quarter-end—six months ahead of schedule. This has unlocked a 17% reduction in our time-to-market for new features, directly contributing to a 32% year-over-year increase in mobile app active users, reaching 14.2 million, or 68% of our total customer base. Transaction volumes via digital channels surged 41% to $1.2 trillion, with API-driven integrations boosting embedded finance revenues by 52% to $450 million annualized.

A standout here is our AI-powered "UniSmart Advisor," our generative AI suite launched in Q1, which now serves 4.8 million users with hyper-personalized recommendations—think real-time cash flow forecasting for SMBs using machine learning models trained on 15 years of anonymized transaction data. Early results mirror JPMorgan's IndexGPT success: customer engagement scores up 24%, cross-sell ratios improved to 3.2 products per customer, and fee income from advisory services grew 29% to $210 million. On the technical front, we're PSD2-compliant in Europe with over 1,200 open banking APIs live, enabling partnerships like our co-branded BNPL product with Klarna, which has originated $2.8 billion in loans YTD at a blended FICO score of 720.

Turning to customer-centric growth, we're laser-focused on deposit franchise fortification and diversified lending. Core deposits grew 12% year-over-year to $285 billion, with a customer acquisition cost down 19% to $145 per new account, thanks to our "UniRewards" loyalty program integrated with Apple Pay and Google Wallet. In consumer banking, mortgage originations hit $18 billion, up 15%, capturing share in a 6.75% 30-year fixed-rate market, while our auto lending portfolio expanded 22% via dealer partnerships, maintaining delinquencies at a pristine 0.89%—well below the industry average of 1.4%. Wealth management AUM reached $420 billion, a 14% increase, driven by our robo-advisory platform, which now manages 35% of flows algorithmically, delivering ROA of 1.2% versus peers' 0.9%. Commercial banking remains robust, with C&I loan commitments up 9% to $110 billion, focused on middle-market tech and renewables, where we've deployed $3.2 billion in ESG-linked facilities.

Our expansion efforts are yielding strong tailwinds. In North America, which represents 62% of revenues, we've gained 150 basis points market share in digital deposits, outpacing Wells Fargo and Bank of America. Europe, at 22% of the mix, saw 18% revenue growth post our €1.2 billion acquisition of a UK challenger bank, navigating Brexit headwinds with CET1 at 13.2% under Basel IV stress tests. APAC is our growth engine: Singapore and India hubs drove 27% loan book expansion to $45 billion, with digital remittances up 55% via UPI integrations, tapping into a $120 billion cross-border market projected to grow 12% CAGR per McKinsey. We're also piloting stablecoin custody services in Hong Kong, eyeing a $2 trillion tokenized asset opportunity by 2030.

Sustainable resilience underpins it all. Our ESG framework, aligned with TCFD and SFDR, has mobilized $15 billion in green bonds and sustainability-linked loans YTD, attracting $8.2 billion in new inflows from impact funds like BlackRock's. Risk management is fortified: we've stress-tested our $50 billion securities portfolio under a +200 basis points rate shock, with unrealized losses down to 1.8% from 4.2% at peak, and our advanced IRB models have kept provisions at 0.95% of loans. Compliance investments, including GenAI ethics guardrails, position us ahead of Dodd-Frank evolution and DORA regulations.

These initiatives drove 11% adjusted EPS growth this quarter. Looking ahead, we'll allocate $1.8 billion in 2025 capex—60% to tech—with targets of 75% digital adoption and 20% fee income growth. We're well-positioned to navigate 2025's projected 25 basis points rate cuts while compounding our competitive moat.

As we wrap up our discussion, let me dive deep into our capital return strategy and outlook. Our fortress balance sheet continues to underpin robust shareholder returns, with a CET1 ratio of 12.8% as of September 30—well above our internal target of 11.5% and the regulatory minimum of 7.0% under Basel III endgame rules. This positions us optimally to navigate macroeconomic headwinds like the persistent inverted yield curve and cooling inflation, while delivering consistent value to shareholders.

Our dividend policy remains the cornerstone of our capital return framework. We've maintained a progressive dividend strategy since the GFC, prioritizing sustainable growth tied to earnings quality and payout discipline. In Q3, we declared a quarterly common stock dividend of $0.62 per share, up 12% year-over-year from $0.55, marking our 53rd consecutive quarterly increase. This brings our trailing twelve-month payout ratio to a prudent 42% of adjusted EPS—squarely within our 40-50% target band, even as we absorbed one-time integration costs from last year's acquisition of Midwest Regional Bank.

Annualized, this equates to a forward yield of approximately 3.7% based on yesterday's close, which is competitive with peers like JPMorgan Chase at 2.8% and Bank of America at 3.2%, but with our superior ROTCE of 14.2% providing ample cushion. Our U.S. consumer and commercial banking segments—which drove 68% of Q3 fee income—are generating the organic capital to support this trajectory. In Europe, where we've expanded via our partnership with Deutsche Bank on cross-border trade finance, regulatory pressures from the ECB's CRR III implementation have tempered growth, but our CET1 buffer there stands at 13.2%, allowing us to maintain parity on dividend remittances.

Our dividend sustainability is further reinforced by our mid-teens EPS growth outlook for 2025, fueled by NIM expansion to 3.65% in Q3 (up 25 basis points quarter-over-quarter) amid higher-for-longer Fed funds rates. We've stress-tested this under our internal scenarios, including a 100 basis points rate cut cycle starting mid-2025, and project payout coverage north of 1.5x even in a mild recession—akin to our CCAR "severely adverse" scenario results from June, where we comfortably passed with zero restrictions.

Shifting to share repurchases, our opportunistic buyback program complements dividends by enhancing EPS accretion and ROE. In the first nine months of 2024, we repurchased 18 million shares, or 2.1% of our float, at an average price of $82.50—totaling $1.5 billion against our $2.5 billion authorization from Q4 2023. This was executed opportunistically during dips tied to summer market volatility from U.S. election uncertainty and Middle East tensions impacting energy markets. Post-repurchase, our tangible book value per share rose 8% year-over-year to $45.20, underscoring the accretive impact.

Our buyback discipline is governed by a clear framework: we target 60-70% of excess capital returns via repurchases when shares trade below 1.1x TBV, which they've done for 65% of trading days this year. This mirrors strategies at Wells Fargo and Citigroup, but with our lower beta (0.85 vs. KBW Bank Index's 1.0), we've avoided the volatility traps that plagued regional peers like KeyCorp during the 2023 banking mini-crisis.

Technologically, we're leveraging our $450 million annual investment in core modernization—including our cloud-native core banking platform migrated to AWS in partnership with FIS—to drive efficiency ratios down to 55% by year-end 2025 from 58% today. This frees up $300-400 million in annual opex savings, directly bolstering deployable capital. In Asia-Pacific, where digital wallets and BNPL products via our JV with Grab have scaled to $15 billion in originations, AI-driven fraud detection has cut losses by 30%, enhancing risk-adjusted returns and supporting localized buyback flexibility under HKMA guidelines.

Strategically, our capital return philosophy balances shareholder generosity with growth investments. Post-CCAR, we've recalibrated our capital plan to allocate 75% of projected 2025 excess capital—estimated at $4.2 billion after organic generation and RWA growth—to returns, with the balance funding selective M&A like our pending $1.2 billion purchase of a Southeast Asian micro-lender to tap underserved SME markets. This is prudent amid Basel IV's output floor hitting in 2026, which could inflate RWAs by 8-10% industry-wide; our proactive RWA optimization via IFRS 9 modeling has mitigated this to just 4%.

Looking to 2025 and beyond, we're announcing today a 15% dividend increase to $0.71 per share quarterly, effective Q1, implying a $2.84 annualized DPS and targeting a 45% payout ratio. Concurrently, we're authorizing a new $3 billion share repurchase program through Q4 2026, with flexibility to accelerate if shares remain undervalued relative to our 11-13x forward P/E peer median. Under base case assumptions—2% U.S. GDP growth, Fed funds at 4.25% term-end, and deposit beta stabilization at 35%—we expect to return $5.8 billion to shareholders, equating to a 9-11% total yield including buyback accretion.

U.S. markets remain our engine, with CRE exposure tightly managed at 210% LTV average and office loans stress-tested to 40% vacancy. Europe faces headwinds from negative deposit rates lingering in select markets, but our 15% year-over-year fee growth in capital markets offsets this. In Asia, regulatory tailwinds like India's UPI expansion position us for 20% loan growth, with capital returns scaled accordingly.

Our capital return plans reflect a shareholder-first mindset, backed by battle-tested stress capital planning and operational excellence. We're committed to compounding value through cycles, much like our track record since IPO in 1998.

Lisa Patel:
Thank you, Michael. As Chief Risk Officer, I would like to briefly discuss our risk management framework. We continue to prioritize proactive risk identification and mitigation. Our key focus areas include credit risk, particularly in commercial real estate amid office sector challenges, and market volatility from geopolitical tensions and rate uncertainty. We remain vigilant in monitoring emerging risks like cyber threats and regulatory changes, adapting our strategies accordingly with advanced stress testing and IRB models.

Operator, we are now ready to open the line for questions.

Operator:
Ladies and gentlemen, at this time we will be conducting a question-and-answer session. [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from John Smith with KBW. Please go ahead.

John Smith:
Good morning. Can you provide more detail on your revenue diversification initiatives?

Sarah Thompson:
Good morning, John. Thanks for the question. As Michael outlined, our diversification has meaningfully shifted our revenue mix to 52% NII and 48% non-interest, with standout growth in WAM, payments, and CIB fees. Initiatives like UniWealth AI and UniPay Nexus are driving inflows and volumes, and we're on track for 15-18% non-interest growth this year. Happy to follow up offline.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Chen with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Emily Chen:
What are your expectations for non-interest income going forward?

Michael Chen:
Hi Emily. We expect $2.7-2.9 billion in Q4, with upside from volatility in trading and potential M&A rebound as rates ease. Our fintech partnerships and AI data monetization should add tailwinds, targeting 5-7% CAGR through the cycle despite market headwinds.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Lee with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

David Lee:
Can you comment on the credit quality of your commercial real estate portfolio?

David Kim:
Good morning, David. Credit quality remains strong overall, with delinquencies low at under 1%. In CRE, we're focused on office exposure, which we've stress-tested to 40% vacancy with provisions at 0.95% of loans. We've deleveraged non-core assets, selling $5 billion, and LTV averages 210%. We're comfortable with the outlook.

Operator:
There are no further questions at this time. I'd like to turn the conference back over to Sarah Thompson for any closing remarks.

Sarah Thompson:
Thank you for your interest in UniBank Group. We appreciate you joining us today. We look forward to speaking with you again next quarter.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
aspects: Capital ratios (CET1, Tier 1): levels and regulatory requirements
Impact of market conditions on non-interest income
Capital return plans (dividends, share repurchases): strategy and outlook
